{"id": "87:16/q12", "question": "How does this verse connect to its surrounding passage and the sūra?", "turns_on": "Whether the emphasis falls on the immediate contrast of 87:14–17, the transition to earlier scriptures, or the sūra's broader address and mission.", "positions": [{"id": "87:16/q12/p1", "position": "It contrasts the earlier call to purification and prayer with preference for the world, then the better and lasting Hereafter.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī takes 'this' in 87:18–19 to refer to nearby 87:14–17, including this verse, because the demonstrative points to the nearest passage; ṣuḥuf means Abraham's and Moses' books or scrolls. Biqāʿī describes an implicit contrast: rejecting the Hereafter follows from preferring the world, and 87:17 implies the world's inferiority. Corpus Coranicum points to the vocabulary of 93:4."}, {"id": "87:16/q12/p2", "position": "The worldly rebuke prepares a warning against abandoning purification outside the prophets' way.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī reads the subsequent development as warning against turning from purification by a path other than the prophets' method."}, {"id": "87:16/q12/p3", "position": "The sūra shifts from addressing the Messenger to confronting hearers with the core choice and its consequences.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum links the abrupt rebuke with 102:1 and says an earlier contrast of good and bad now becomes a direct choice. It argues second-person rebukes and parallel growth of text and community make a presupposed formed community or follower-only devotional meetings unlikely."}, {"id": "87:16/q12/p4", "position": "The sūra frames worldly preference within its themes of revelation, divine oneness and final recompense.", "reasons": "Quṭb calls al-Aʿlā Meccan with nineteen verses, loved and recited by the Prophet at Eid and Friday prayer alongside al-Ghāshiya, sometimes the same day. He describes cosmic praise, promised preservation and ease for the Messenger, earlier scriptures in 87:18–19, and the easy nature of the message and community."}, {"id": "87:16/q12/p5", "position": "Attachment to transient interests explains why the Prophet's message does not take root among its hearers.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says disbelievers cling to passing life despite prophetic continuity, and Quraysh invent doubts rather than risk worldly interests for eternal reward."}]}
{"id": "87:16/q13", "question": "What does the direct address imply about human choice?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:16/q13/p1", "position": "Choosing worldly life is an act of the human subjects addressed.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī argues that the direct 'you prefer' attributes this choice to the people themselves."}]}
{"id": "87:17/q01", "question": "What does al-ākhirah designate here?", "turns_on": "Whether al-ākhirah is taken broadly as the next abode, specifically as Paradise, or inwardly as spiritual life.", "positions": [{"id": "87:17/q01/p1", "position": "The life or abode after this world.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Nasafī and others contrast it with worldly life; al-Biqāʿī calls it the exalted abode and goal of creation and command."}, {"id": "87:17/q01/p2", "position": "Paradise or the Garden.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Qurṭubī explicitly gloss the afterlife as Paradise; Ibn al-Jawzī specifies the Garden for the Prophet."}, {"id": "87:17/q01/p3", "position": "The true spiritual life with God.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī contrasts it with sensory life and its ornaments, linking worldly preference to neglected remembrance and prayer and lack of purification."}]}
{"id": "87:17/q02", "question": "In what sense is the Hereafter better than worldly life?", "turns_on": "The notes variously state a general comparison or specify its beneficiary as believers, the obedient and Paradise's people, or the Prophet.", "positions": [{"id": "87:17/q02/p1", "position": "It surpasses worldly life in goodness, pleasure, and reward.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī and Qatāda say better in goodness; al-Kashshāf, al-Nasafī and Qutb stress intrinsic or qualitative superiority. Al-Jishumī, al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Biqāʿī, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī say its pleasure is pure or unspoiled whereas worldly pleasure is slight, interrupted or mixed with pain; al-Rāzī adds bodily and spiritual happiness; Ibn Kathīr calls the world low and the next abode noble. Al-Biqāʿī calls its bliss the goal of creation and command. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says relative superiority suffices for the comparison."}, {"id": "87:17/q02/p2", "position": "It is better in its recompense for believers or those who seek it.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī specifies believers and enduring recompense; al-Qushayrī specifies believers who seek it."}, {"id": "87:17/q02/p3", "position": "It is better for the obedient, and its permanence belongs to the people of Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī presents this as a synthesis or further possibility, assigning the two predicates to those two groups respectively."}, {"id": "87:17/q02/p4", "position": "The Garden is better and more lasting for the Prophet.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī's formulation singles out the Prophet as beneficiary."}]}
{"id": "87:17/q03", "question": "What does abqā say about duration?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:17/q03/p1", "position": "The afterlife lasts longer than the passing world, ultimately without end.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī and Qatāda contrast this life's ending with the next life's permanence. Al-Rāzī and al-Biqāʿī argue that permanence outranks transience; al-Biqāʿī says even a prolonged world is only figuratively lasting. Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies abqā as a comparative of longer duration and cites the Prophet's garment saying as parallel usage. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes the comparative claim from the afterlife's intrinsic eternity; al-Samīn identifies worldly life as the omitted thing surpassed. Al-Itqān compares another omitted comparative, 'what is more hidden.'"}]}
{"id": "87:17/q04", "question": "How is this clause grammatically construed?", "turns_on": "These are compatible analyses of sentence form, its relation to 87:16, and comparative ellipsis.", "positions": [{"id": "87:17/q04/p1", "position": "It is a nominal sentence with a subject and predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās analyzes al-ākhiratu khayrun wa-abqā this way."}, {"id": "87:17/q04/p2", "position": "It functions as a circumstantial clause attached to the subject of 'you prefer.'", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says this construction reinforces the rebuke of 87:16."}, {"id": "87:17/q04/p3", "position": "The comparatives leave worldly life unstated as what is surpassed.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn supplies worldly life for abqā; al-Itqān gives this verse and 'knows the secret and what is more hidden' as examples of an omitted comparative term."}]}
{"id": "87:17/q05", "question": "Why does this wording leave parts of the contrast implicit?", "turns_on": "The authors explain the implied worldly contrast through rhetorical pairing or through the obviousness of worldly defects.", "positions": [{"id": "87:17/q05/p1", "position": "The paired clauses imply rejection and elevation after worldly preference, and the world's defects after the Hereafter's goodness; the order first deters, then attracts.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī explains both sides of the ellipsis and the sequence of deterrence followed by attraction."}, {"id": "87:17/q05/p2", "position": "The world's troubled pleasure and short span are omitted because they are obvious.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the listeners already know these defects."}]}
{"id": "87:17/q06", "question": "Why do people prefer worldly life despite this comparison?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize present visibility, inward disposition, or the disbelievers' concrete worldly interests.", "positions": [{"id": "87:17/q06/p1", "position": "Its pleasures are present and visible, while the promised afterlife is hidden or deferred.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd names immediate food, drink, women, pleasure and adornment, contrasted with an unseen promised afterlife; the reports vary between his confession at the verse and a fuller list of pleasures. Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds ignorance of the afterlife's permanence; Qatāda says only those God protects escape this choice."}, {"id": "87:17/q06/p2", "position": "Low aspiration, attachment to appearances, and lack of purification veil the lasting life.", "reasons": "Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Dīnawarī contrasts low and elevated ambition; al-Qāshānī links attachment to sensory ornaments with neglected remembrance and prayer; al-Bursawī describes outward-looking people as veiled from the Hereafter."}, {"id": "87:17/q06/p3", "position": "Disbelievers, especially Quraysh, protect worldly interests even at the expense of eternal reward.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says their attachment makes the Prophet's message fail to take root; Quraysh invent doubts rather than risk their interests."}]}
{"id": "87:17/q07", "question": "What choice and conduct does the comparison call for?", "turns_on": "The sources prescribe choosing the lasting reward, name its preparatory acts, or describe the highest aspiration as seeking God beyond both worlds.", "positions": [{"id": "87:17/q07/p1", "position": "Choose and seek the enduring Hereafter over worldly life.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reasons that what is better and more enduring deserves preference; Ibn Kathīr calls such a choice rational. Al-Biqāʿī urges rejecting sensory attractions and imagined pleasures. Al-Bursawī says preferring mixed, temporary pleasure merits rebuke; Qutb calls the reverse foolish judgment. Mālik ibn Dīnār's illustration values even lasting pottery over passing gold. Al-Māwardī and al-Qushayrī specify faithful seekers; Kur'an Yolu warns unbelievers and believers, citing 7:169, 12:109 and 93:4."}, {"id": "87:17/q07/p2", "position": "Work for purification, charity, remembrance and prayer in preparation to meet God.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says worldly preference ends in loss, while afterlife seekers can bear hards

hip without despair, seek escape from pain and God's pleasure rather than mere survival, and give obligatory charity, remember the Lord and pray."}, {"id": "87:17/q07/p3", "position": "Seek the Lord above both worldly life and the afterlife.", "reasons": "Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Dīnawarī distinguishes noble states and sound realities from the merely elevated ambition that chooses the afterlife."}]}
{"id": "87:17/q08", "question": "What reported images convey the world's value beside the Hereafter?", "turns_on": "These are distinct reported analogies or sayings, with different speakers and images.", "positions": [{"id": "87:17/q08/p1", "position": "The world is like a rabbit's sneeze or puff of breath beside the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf and Ibn ʿAṭiyya report ʿUmar's image; wording varies between sneeze and puff of breath."}, {"id": "87:17/q08/p2", "position": "The world is like water brought back by a finger dipped in the sea.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports the Prophet's comparison and calls the hadith sound or authentic."}, {"id": "87:17/q08/p3", "position": "Even passing gold would be inferior to lasting pottery, while in truth the Hereafter is lasting gold and the world passing pottery.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports Mālik ibn Dīnār's counterfactual comparison."}, {"id": "87:17/q08/p4", "position": "The world is home and wealth for those lacking real home and wealth, amassed by the mindless.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr attributes this to the Prophet through ʿĀʾisha and says Aḥmad transmits it; al-Durr likewise reports it."}, {"id": "87:17/q08/p5", "position": "The world is a prison for the believer and a garden for the disbeliever.", "reasons": "The Study Quran cites a Prophetic hadith and mentions 93:4."}, {"id": "87:17/q08/p6", "position": "God created nothing more hated to Him than the world and has never looked at it.", "reasons": "Al-Durr reports this through Mūsā ibn Yasār."}]}
{"id": "87:17/q09", "question": "What reported counsel addresses love of the two lives?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in whether they give reciprocal counsel about the two lives or a caveat about testimony and worldly attachment.", "positions": [{"id": "87:17/q09/p1", "position": "Love of either life harms one's share in the other, so choose what endures.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī transmits the reciprocal warning; Ibn Kathīr reports Abū Mūsā's Prophetic version and notes Aḥmad alone transmits it, also through another route; al-Durr repeats the counsel."}, {"id": "87:17/q09/p2", "position": "The testimony leading to Paradise is compromised by love, preference, accumulation and contentment with worldly life and tyrannical conduct.", "reasons": "Al-Durr gives this as a Prophetic report in the notes on both 87:16 and 87:17."}]}
{"id": "87:17/q10", "question": "How is the preceding verb of preference read?", "turns_on": "Whether 87:16 addresses 'you' or speaks of 'they'; Ṭabarī cites reader consensus and Ubayy's antum for the second person.", "positions": [{"id": "87:17/q10/p1", "position": "In the second person, addressing the hearers.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers the readers' consensus on this reading and cites Ubayy's recitation with antum before the verb as support."}, {"id": "87:17/q10/p2", "position": "In the third person with yāʾ, referring to the wretched.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī reports Abū ʿAmr's reading; al-Durr reports that Ibn Masʿūd also read the verb with yāʾ."}]}
{"id": "87:17/q11", "question": "Which teaching here belongs to the earlier scriptures?", "turns_on": "Whether 'this' in the next verses points to the nearby passage as a whole or specifically to 87:17; Ṭabarī appeals to the nearest referent.", "positions": [{"id": "87:17/q11/p1", "position": "The nearby passage from purification and prayer through the afterlife comparison belongs to them.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers 87:14–17 as the nearest referent of 'this' and says ṣuḥuf means the books or scrolls of Abraham and Moses. Al-Kalbī takes it from 'successful is one who purifies' through the sūra's end; al-Bursawī includes reward, soul purification, knowledge, obedience and warning against worldly distraction. A report says the Prophet recited this passage when asked what he received from the scrolls."}, {"id": "87:17/q11/p2", "position": "The specific teaching is that the afterlife is better and more enduring than worldly life.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd limits 'this' to the comparison; Qatāda says God's books repeatedly or successively teach it, including the earlier scrolls. Iṣlāḥī says the Prophet's message continues earlier prophetic teaching."}]}
{"id": "87:17/q12", "question": "How does this verse work in the sūra's argument?", "turns_on": "These notes trace different connections: immediate rebuke, purification and prophetic teaching, or the sūra's broader movement.", "positions": [{"id": "87:17/q12/p1", "position": "It reinforces the rebuke of worldly preference by stating the better, lasting alternative.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says it exposes what the audience ignored; al-Ālūsī describes its circumstantial force. Corpus Coranicum sees a shift from address to the messenger into direct rebuke of hearers and a choice with eschatological consequences, mentioning 102:1. Kur'an Yolu connects 7:169, 12:109 and 93:4; Corpus Coranicum points to 93:4 for this vocabulary."}, {"id": "87:17/q12/p2", "position": "It connects the warning against worldly preference with purification and the prophetic path.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says the sūra proceeds to warn against turning from purification through routes other than the prophets' method; Qutb says the sūra grounds afterlife recompense in earlier scripture, beside God's oneness and revelation, and portrays an easy message, messenger and community."}, {"id": "87:17/q12/p3", "position": "The sūra's wider movement contrasts good and bad and brings hearers to a consequential choice.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum says the contrast turns from an earlier typology to the listeners and argues that second-person rebukes and the parallel growth of text and community do not presuppose a formed community or only follower meetings. Qutb describes the cosmos as a sanctuary of praise and divine support for the Prophet; Iṣlāḥī says worldly attachment keeps the message from taking root."}]}
{"id": "87:17/q13", "question": "What sūra setting and recitation are reported alongside this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:17/q13/p1", "position": "Al-Aʿlā is Meccan, has nineteen verses, and the Prophet loved and recited it at Eid and Friday prayers with al-Ghāshiya, sometimes on the same day.", "reasons": "Qutb gives this sūra information and mentions 88:1."}]}
{"id": "87:17/q14", "question": "How do inward readings describe the lasting life?", "turns_on": "The inward notes emphasize true spiritual life, the inner kernel, or devotion to the Lord beyond both worlds.", "positions": [{"id": "87:17/q14/p1", "position": "True spiritual life, gained through purification, remembrance and prayer, outlasts sensory life.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī connects the sensory world's ornaments with neglect of remembrance and prayer."}, {"id": "87:17/q14/p2", "position": "Inner reality is the lasting kernel; outward appearance is a quickly discarded shell.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī uses the kernel and shell analogy and says people of inner truth choose the lasting life with God while outward-looking people are veiled."}, {"id": "87:17/q14/p3", "position": "The highest aspiration prefers the Lord over both worlds.", "reasons": "Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Dīnawarī ranks low worldly ambition, elevated afterlife ambition, and noble states or sound realities that seek God."}]}
{"id": "87:18/q01", "question": "What does “this” refer to?", "turns_on": "Which earlier material the demonstrative reaches: the nearest statement, the adjacent passage, the whole sūra, or the Qurʾān; proximity and the reported sayings are offered as tests.", "positions": [{"id": "87:18/q01/p1", "position": "The teaching in verses 14–17: purification, remembrance, prayer, worldly preference, and the better, lasting afterlife.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Abū Ḥayyān, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya favor proximity; Ibn Kathīr calls this a strong choice. Rāzī reads the sequence as purification of belief and morals, knowledge of God, bodily obedience, and release from worldly attachment. Abū Dharr's report is cited for the span; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the opening through verse 13 is not confirmed here and cannot grade that report."}, {"id": "87:18/q01/p2", "position": "The whole sūra, its story, teachings, or verses.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says it was copied; al-Suddī says it appeared as revealed to Muhammad. Rāzī says the sūra covers oneness, prophecy, warning and promise. Ibn Qutayba denies that its entire meaning or exact wording must be present. Al-Ālūsī calls this broad reference remote."}, {"id": "87:18/q01/p3", "position": "Only the nearest statement that the afterlife is better and more lasting.", "reasons": "Qatāda and Ibn Zayd say God's books repeat this teaching; al-Naḥḥās and Rāzī appeal to the nearest antecedent. Al-Ṭabarī instead takes all nearby verses."}, {"id": "87:18/q01/p4", "position": "The teaching of purification, remembrance, prayer, and success in verses 14–15.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba limits the common teaching to these verses; al-Naḥḥās reports the same, while al-Bayḍāwī says the promise of success sums up religion. Al-Ālūsī cites a later hadith."}, {"id": "87:18/q01/p5", "position": "The Qurʾān as a whole.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk is repeatedly credited with this view; al-Ālūsī and Study Quran compare 26:196. A report says the Qurʾān was transcribed from earlier scriptures."}, {"id": "87:18/q01/p6", "position": "The admonition to obey and avoid sin, or to prefer the hereafter.", "reasons": "Jishumī attributes the preference reading to Abū ʿAlī and reports an obedience and sin reading alongside Abū Muslim's account of commands to earlier communities."}, {"id": "87:18/q01/p7"

, "position": "The broader warning and promise from verse 9 through verse 17.", "reasons": "Nasafī gives this span as an alternative; Qāshānī includes receptive and unreceptive hearers, flourishing purified people, and those ruined by sensory life."}, {"id": "87:18/q01/p8", "position": "The great admonition shared by these sūras, beginning with glorification.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī includes glorification, purification, remembrance, prayer, and turning toward the afterlife as the unalterable goal of every revealed law."}, {"id": "87:18/q01/p9", "position": "The teachings across all sūras.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī attributes this to Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, and al-Suddī but considers it far-fetched."}]}
{"id": "87:18/q02", "question": "In what sense is this teaching “in” the earlier scriptures?", "turns_on": "Whether being written earlier entails shared teaching or actual transcription and verbal correspondence.", "positions": [{"id": "87:18/q02/p1", "position": "Its meaning or counterpart is there, though the wording and language may differ.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba excludes an exact verbal identity; al-Kashshāf, Nasafī, al-Ālūsī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr specify shared meaning. Ibn ʿĀshūr takes scrolls as a container metonymy, comparing 38:16."}, {"id": "87:18/q02/p2", "position": "The sūra was copied or transcribed from earlier scrolls, even appearing as revealed to Muhammad.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās's reported wording says copied; al-Suddī makes the stronger claim of correspondence as revealed. Another report extends this to the end of Sūra 53."}]}
{"id": "87:18/q03", "question": "What does ṣuḥuf mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:18/q03/p1", "position": "Written sheets or scrolls, plural of ṣaḥīfa; by extension, books of revelation.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and al-Thaʿlabī give the plural. Bursawī distinguishes a muṣḥaf as a collection of sheets. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls ṣuḥuf an eloquent irregular plural, like sufun from safīna; Kuran Yolu says it became synonymous with book. Corpus Coranicum suggests Old South Arabian borrowing and notes the early Qurʾānic revelatory sense, later largely replaced by kitāb, alongside zubur."}]}
{"id": "87:18/q04", "question": "How is the ḥāʾ of ṣuḥuf read?", "turns_on": "The vowel of the ḥāʾ, with sukūn identified as a Tamīm dialect.", "positions": [{"id": "87:18/q04/p1", "position": "With ḍamma on the ḥāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān assign this to the majority."}, {"id": "87:18/q04/p2", "position": "With sukūn on the ḥāʾ, here and sometimes in the next verse.", "reasons": "Reported from al-Aʿmash and from Abū ʿAmr through Hārūn and ʿIṣmah; Abū Ḥayyān's al-Lawāmiʿ and al-Ālūsī call it Tamīmī usage. Al-Samīn says the form is straightforward."}]}
{"id": "87:18/q05", "question": "Which scriptures are meant by the earlier scrolls?", "turns_on": "Whether the named prophets possessed scrolls, exemplify all revelation, or evoke biblical writings.", "positions": [{"id": "87:18/q05/p1", "position": "Abraham's scrolls and Moses's books, especially the Torah.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī names the two; Muqātil says Abraham's scrolls have been taken away. Ibn ʿĀshūr says Moses had many scrolls comprising Torah books. Kuran Yolu treats them as examples of prophetic revelation, not its limits."}, {"id": "87:18/q05/p2", "position": "All of God's earlier revealed books.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan says the teaching occurs in all God's books; al-Māwardī gives this as a third interpretation. The claim is about the reach of the plural, beyond the two named exemplars."}, {"id": "87:18/q05/p3", "position": "A broad evocation of biblical scripture through Abraham and Moses.", "reasons": "Ahrens calls it a rough label for the Old Testament or whole Bible, citing 53:36 onward. Corpus Coranicum prefers a biblical summary through prominent figures and finds specific apocryphal Abrahamic books unlikely; it notes the Old Testament has no revealed Abrahamic book. Heck reads writings about the figures through an objective genitive, which Corpus Coranicum does not adopt."}, {"id": "87:18/q05/p4", "position": "Revealed writings about Moses and Abraham.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum reports Heck's objective genitive analysis, but its author prefers a broad biblical evocation."}]}
{"id": "87:18/q06", "question": "How many scrolls or revealed books were given, and to whom?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in their totals and in whether Adam or Moses receives ten preliminary scrolls, and whether Abraham receives ten or twenty.", "positions": [{"id": "87:18/q06/p1", "position": "104 books: ten sheets to Adam, fifty to Seth, thirty to Idrīs, ten to Abraham, plus four named books.", "reasons": "Abū Dharr's account in al-Thaʿlabī and al-Kashshāf gives this allocation; al-Thaʿlabī adds that Idrīs first wrote with a pen. Kuran Yolu repeats the ten, fifty, thirty, ten distribution."}, {"id": "87:18/q06/p2", "position": "104 books: fifty to Seth, thirty to Idrīs, ten to Abraham, ten to Moses before the Torah, then four named books.", "reasons": "Abū Dharr's prophetic account gives this distribution in al-Durr; Study Quran reports it and notes Shiite variants."}, {"id": "87:18/q06/p3", "position": "105 scrolls and four books: thirty-five to Seth, fifty to Idrīs, twenty to Abraham.", "reasons": "Wahb ibn Munabbih names the four later books for Moses, David, Jesus, and Muhammad; Study Quran says some reports assign Abraham twenty scrolls."}, {"id": "87:18/q06/p4", "position": "A total of 104 revealed books, without an allocation in this note.", "reasons": "Jishumī says the books were apportioned among a list of prophets; Shiite sources have a slightly different narration according to Study Quran."}]}
{"id": "87:18/q07", "question": "When were these and other scriptures revealed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:18/q07/p1", "position": "Abraham's scrolls on Ramadan's first night; Torah on the sixth, Psalms on the twelfth, Gospel on the eighteenth, and Furqān on the twenty-fourth.", "reasons": "Abū al-Khald gives this sequence in both Ṭabarī versions."}]}
{"id": "87:18/q08", "question": "What do reports say Abraham's scrolls taught?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:18/q08/p1", "position": "Practical maxims for wise people and rulers.", "reasons": "The sayings counsel guarding tongue and time, attending to one's affairs, worship, self-examination, lawful needs and livelihood, and answering the oppressed even when unbelieving; Abū Dharr's report also warns rulers against hoarding."}]}
{"id": "87:18/q09", "question": "What do reports say Moses's scrolls taught?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:18/q09/p1", "position": "Admonitions about mortality, worldly change, destiny, and judgment.", "reasons": "Abū Dharr's prophetic account challenges joy despite death, trust amid change, striving as though destiny were unknown, and failure to act despite certain judgment."}]}
{"id": "87:18/q10", "question": "What is said about the survival of Abraham's and Moses's teachings?", "turns_on": "Whether the earlier teachings survived as scrolls, in later writings, or as enduring principles across laws.", "positions": [{"id": "87:18/q10/p1", "position": "The central teachings persisted through every revealed law without abrogation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān apply this to purification and the afterlife; Rāzī says reason and transmission show these truths do not vary; al-Biqāʿī says the aim of all laws cannot be abrogated.
